title: Ravidas Dreams Begampura
subtitle: A cobbler-poet carves a city beyond fear from the dust of Banaras
era: North Indian Sant tradition, c. 15th-early 16th century CE
region: Varanasi and the Banaras leather-working world
moral: The future begins when someone dares to name a fairer city.

sources.citation: Guru Granth Sahib, Ravidas bani, 41 hymns
sources.note: Best-authenticated early corpus of Ravidas's verses, fixed by 1604.

sources.citation: Panch Vani and related Dadu Panthi anthologies
sources.note: Additional Ravidas traditions with source-critical debates.

sources.citation: John Stratton Hawley and Mark Juergensmeyer, Songs of the Saints of India (1988/2004); Hawley, A Storm of Songs (2015); Purushottam Agrawal, Akath Kahani Prem Ki (2009)
sources.note: Critical studies of Sant poetry, manuscript transmission and social context.

panels.shot: wide, low-angle dusk view of Ravidas at his roadside cobbler stall, city of Banaras hazy behind him like a distant fortress

dialogue.text: In fifteenth-century Banaras, where caste ruled every doorway, a cobbler named Ravidas dared to sing of Begampura—a city with no fear, no taxes, no second-class souls.

panels.shot: slow push-in from street chaos to intimate close-up of Ravidas’s hands working leather

dialogue.text: The records do not give us Ravidas’s exact birth year. They give us something sharper—his voice, rising from Banaras’ leather-working world, where Chamars laboured at the edge of respect.

panels.shot: medium shot, Ravidas seated at his stall, brahmin customers passing by him with subtle distance

dialogue.text: To mend shoes was to carry the mark of leather, of impurity, in a world of strict hierarchies. But Ravidas did not only shape sandals. He shaped questions—about who truly belongs.

panels.shot: interior hut, close-up of Ravidas’s face lit by lamp as he chants, background simple family space

dialogue.text: From this small, dim space in Banaras came songs that crossed regions. The Guru Granth Sahib preserves forty-one of them—words that carried the weight of a cobbler’s life and a seeker’s fire.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot of Ravidas by the Ganga ghats, priests and commoners around, subtle distance between him and ritual center

dialogue.text: In the north Indian Sant tradition, Ravidas’s voice joined those who turned from ritual to inner devotion. Yet his path was marked by something more—life under caste exclusion, felt every day.

panels.shot: close-up on Ravidas’s eyes, background dissolving into faint outlines of palaces and tax collectors

dialogue.text: Cities promised safety, wealth, splendour. They also brought anxiety—taxes, tolls, the fear of guards at every gate. For a low-caste cobbler, the city was shelter and cage at once.

panels.shot: intimate shot inside hut, Ravidas composing, a palm-leaf manuscript nearby, his tools set aside

dialogue.text: And so Ravidas began to sing of another city. Not Banaras with its taxes, or fort towns with guarded walls—but Begampura, a place that broke the old rules of belonging.

panels.shot: semi-symbolic wide shot, Ravidas seated, with a faint visionary city forming around him in light

dialogue.text: Begampura shahar ko nāu… dukhu andohu nahi tihī thāu.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Ravidas, visionary streets showing people of many backgrounds walking together

dialogue.text: “Begampura, that is the name of the town; there is no suffering there, no fear.” In his verse, no one trembles before tax men, no one is pushed aside as less than whole.

panels.shot: medium shot, Ravidas singing to a small, mixed gathering of workers and ordinary folk in a lane

dialogue.text: Begampura is not a blueprint for bricks and stone. It is a challenge: can a city exist without second-class citizens, without the tight fist of revenue and caste at every turn?

panels.shot: close-up of a listener’s face, moved, then back to Ravidas’s steady presence

dialogue.text: In a world where most accepted caste as fate, Ravidas’s words bent that future. He did not draft laws; he named a city where fear itself had no right to live.

panels.shot: symbolic split scene, one half showing royal tax collection, other half Begampura’s open gate

dialogue.text: Ravidas speaks of a place where kings do not impose crushing levies, where no one is harassed for dues. His city is less a place on a map than a measure of justice.

panels.shot: medium shot of Ravidas declining reverence, seated plainly among listeners

dialogue.text: Later stories would wrap Ravidas with more miracles, more royal visits, more disciples. Scholars sift these tales with care—but Begampura stands firm in the older, attested songs.

panels.shot: interior scriptorium-style scene, anonymous scribes copying verses, Ravidas’s figure faintly in background

dialogue.text: By 1604, when the Guru Granth Sahib was compiled, forty-one hymns of Ravidas had travelled far enough, reliably enough, to be gathered into Sikh scripture as part of a shared spiritual canon.

panels.shot: close-up on a manuscript leaf showing Ravidas’s name and lines of verse, hands reverently turning it

dialogue.text: From Banaras’ leather lanes to the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib, his words crossed boundaries that his body could not. The cobbler’s song became part of everyday prayer.

panels.shot: modern symbolic montage: faint outlines of contemporary Ravidassia gathering overlaying Ravidas singing

dialogue.text: Today, communities who honour Ravidas wrestle with his legacy, with identity and dignity. Historians trace transmission lines; devotees hear in Begampura a promise still not fully kept.

panels.shot: wide shot of Ravidas back at his stall, visionary Begampura hovering above the city like a gentle mirage

dialogue.text: No stone city of Begampura was ever founded. Yet every time someone refuses fear and exclusion, they walk a little of its streets—the ones a cobbler once dared to name from the margins.
